nameStory: The name "lingonberry" comes from the Swedish word "lingon," which has been used for centuries in Scandinavia where these berries are a cherished part of traditional cuisine. You might also hear it called "partridgeberry" because grouse and other game birds love to feast on the bright red fruits, or "mountain cranberry" since it grows in higher, cooler places than its bog-dwelling cranberry cousins.
description: Lingonberry is a low-growing evergreen shrub that rarely gets taller than your ankle, usually staying under 8 inches high. This hardy little plant spreads by underground runners to form small colonies of glossy, dark green leaves that stay put year-round. In summer, it produces clusters of tiny white or pale pink bell-shaped flowers, followed by bright red berries that look like miniature cranberries. Think of it as the northern cousin of cranberry that prefers mountains to bogs.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval evergreen leaves about the size of your thumbnail with a distinctive leathery feel and glossy dark green surface. Turn them over to see tiny black dots scattered across the pale underside - these are actually glands that help identify lingonberry from other small-leaved plants.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about the size of small peas that hang in clusters from branch tips. They feel firm when ripe and have a tart, slightly bitter taste - much more acidic than blueberries but similar to cranberries.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bell-shaped flowers, pure white or tinged with pink, that dangle in small clusters of 2-8 blooms. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch long and feels waxy to the touch, with the classic downward-facing shape of heath family flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely growing taller than 6-8 inches. The plants spread by underground stems to create colonies, so you'll often find patches rather than individual plants.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Tiny woody stems have thin, reddish-brown bark that feels smooth to the touch. The stems are wiry and flexible, bending rather than breaking when pressed.

habitat: Look for lingonberry in New England's cooler, higher elevation areas - mountain slopes, exposed ridgetops, and rocky outcrops where the soil is acidic and well-drained. It thrives in the same harsh conditions where you might find blueberries, bunchberry, and mountain ash, often growing among granite boulders or in thin soil over bedrock. In our region, it's most common in the mountains of Vermont, New Hampshire, and western Massachusetts.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright green shoot tips emerging from last year's stems, and the plant maintains its evergreen leaves through the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer with clusters of white bell-shaped flowers, followed by green berries that gradually ripen to bright red by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Berries reach full ripeness and intense red color, often persisting on the plants well into autumn. The evergreen leaves may take on slightly reddish tints in cold weather.
seasonality.winter: The glossy evergreen leaves remain visible above snow, often with dried berries still clinging to stems, making it one of the few green plants you can spot in winter mountain landscapes.

funFact: Lingonberries contain natural benzoic acid, which acts as a preservative - this means you can make lingonberry sauce without adding any sugar or preservatives, and it will keep for months just sitting in your refrigerator, a trick Scandinavian cooks have known for generations!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wintergreen, which also has small evergreen leaves and red berries, but wintergreen leaves smell distinctly minty when crushed while lingonberry leaves have no strong scent. Remember: "Wintergreen means minty scene, lingonberry leaves smell-free."
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this plant with the completely unrelated partridgeberry (Mitchella repens) that grows in lower elevation forests - they share a common name but are in different plant families entirely. True lingonberry is much more rare in New England and grows in totally different habitats.
compareHints: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter. The berries are much more tart than sweet blueberries and lack the distinctive crown that cranberries have. Lingonberry also grows in drier, higher elevation sites compared to bog cranberries and is much lower-growing than highbush blueberries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries.
Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves.
Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants.
Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves.

Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
